claims.claim: An emotion is a subjective state of being — what we often describe as feelings — that results from the combination of subjective experience, expression, cognitive appraisal, and physiological responses; in plain terms, a complex reaction involving the body, the mind, and behavior at once.

The components of emotion are physiological responses (automatic body changes such as heart rate, breathing, and sweating), cognitive appraisal (the evaluation of how a situation affects you), and emotional expression (nonverbal and verbal behaviors that display the emotion).

The classic list of basic emotions names six — happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust — and lists vary by theory: OpenStax Psychology 2e presents seven universal facial expressions, adding contempt (Ekman & Keltner, 1997), and constructivist accounts (e.g., Lisa Feldman Barrett) argue emotions are built from experience rather than hardwired.

The James-Lange theory of emotion (named for William James and Carl Lange) asserts that emotions arise from physiological arousal: the body reacts first, and the feeling of the emotion is the experience of that bodily reaction.

The Cannon-Bard theory of emotion (developed in response to the James-Lange view; Walter Cannon's 1927 critique) asserts that physiological arousal and emotional experience occur simultaneously and independently.

The Schachter-Singer two-factor theory holds that emotions are composed of physiological arousal plus a cognitive label: arousal is interpreted using the context to produce the emotional experience; the 1962 adrenaline experiment (euphoric versus angry confederate) supported the account.

Emotion and mood differ: an emotion is a relatively intense affective state that occurs in response to something we experience (short and specific), while a mood is a prolonged, less intense affective state that does not occur in response to something specific (long and diffuse).

Faces and bodies signal emotion: recognition and production of facial expressions of emotion appear universal (Ekman's New Guinea research; people born blind produce the same expressions; Darwin, 1872), and bodies communicate emotion through posture, movement, and tone (body language).

Expression varies by culture: display rules are culturally specific standards that govern which emotions may be displayed, when, and to whom (e.g., Matsumoto's finding that Americans expressed negative emotions alone and in company while Japanese participants mainly did so alone; the tongue-biting embarrassment signal in India).

Emotions function as rapid information-processing systems that help people act with minimal thinking (Tooby & Cosmides, 2008, as presented by the Noba Project's Functions of Emotions module); the lesson's honest framing is that emotion is data — information about what matters to a person — not noise.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The list of basic emotions varies across theories.
positions: Classic Ekman list: six basic emotions — happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust.
OpenStax Psychology 2e presents seven universal facial expressions: happiness, surprise, sadness, fright, disgust, contempt, anger (Ekman & Keltner, 1997).
Constructivist accounts (Lisa Feldman Barrett) hold that emotions are not hardwired at birth but constructed from experience and prediction.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the classic six as the standard list and states the honest note that lists vary by theory, citing OpenStax's seven-expression set and the constructivist challenge.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The order in which emotion's components occur is unsettled.
positions: James-Lange: physiological arousal precedes and produces the emotion.
Cannon-Bard: physiological arousal and emotional experience occur simultaneously and independently.
Schachter-Singer two-factor: arousal plus a context-based cognitive label produces the emotion.
Appraisal theories (Arnold, Lazarus): cognitive appraisal precedes the emotion.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents all accounts as competing theories without declaring a winner, matching OpenStax's framing that the exact order is not clear and some parts may happen at the same time.

sourceRecords.title: OpenStax Psychology 2e, Section 10.4: Emotion
sourceRecords.notes: Canonical openstax.org URL registered; openstax.org blocks direct fetch, so the section was read via Internet Archive Wayback capture 20210413205843 of the canonical URL. Supports: the working definition (an emotion as a subjective state of being, feelings, resulting from the combination of subjective experience, expression, cognitive appraisal, and physiological responses); the components (physiological responses, cognitive appraisal, emotional expression); emotion versus mood (relatively intense, in response to something, versus prolonged, less intense, not tied to a trigger); the James-Lange, Cannon-Bard, and Schachter-Singer two-factor theories and the 1962 adrenaline experiment; appraisal theory (Arnold, Lazarus); Ekman's New Guinea research and the seven universal expressions (happiness, surprise, sadness, fright, disgust, contempt, anger; Ekman & Keltner, 1997); people born blind producing the same expressions; Darwin (1872); body language; cultural display rules (Malatesta & Haviland, 1982; Matsumoto, 1990); Barrett's constructivist view. Facts synthesized in original wording; no textbook prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Noba Project — Functions of Emotions (Hyisung Hwang & David Matsumoto)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: emotions as rapid information-processing systems that help us act with minimal thinking (Tooby & Cosmides, 2008); the evolutionary function of emotions in solving recurring problems (flee, fight, care, reject, approach); facial expressions of emotion as universal social signals carrying meaning about the expressor's state and intent; the James-Lange theory named in W. B. Cannon's 1927 paper title. Used for the honest framing (emotion as information) and the universality claim. Facts synthesized; no module prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Noba Project — Culture and Emotion (Jeanne Tsai, Stanford University)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: display rules as rules about what emotions are appropriate to show in a given situation (Ekman, 1972); widespread cultural differences in display rules demonstrated by Matsumoto and colleagues (Safdar et al., 2009); the tongue-biting embarrassment signal in India versus no such meaning in the U.S. (Haidt & Keltner, 1999); cultural variation in how emotions are valued and expressed. Used for the honest note that expression varies by culture. Facts synthesized; no module prose reproduced.
